Hi friends. Happy Thursday. 

Today’s episode is personal. It’s painful. And it’s important. We’re talking about the Armenian Genocide... a dark chapter of history that millions experienced, yet many still deny or have never been taught.

I’ve always known I wanted to cover this story because of my family history. But every time I tried, it never felt like the right moment. The truth is… there is no “right moment.” The right thing is to remember, to learn, and to honor those who lived through it... and those who didn’t.

In today's episode, we'll look at how the Armenian community in the Ottoman Empire was targeted, how the genocide was carried out under the chaos of World War I, the stories of survival and resistance, and why recognition of these events is still debated today.

History isn’t always pretty. But understanding it helps us recognize injustice when we see it... and stop it before it happens again.

My great grandmother and her siblings survived the Great Fire of Smyrna that killed thousands of Greeks and Armenians in 1922. Greeks, Armenians, and even Turkish citizens lived together in Smyrna in peace and prosperity until the Ottoman Empire decided to take the whole city. There are books written on the fires, there’s video, there are pictures and still many Turks say that we started the fires ourselves. It’s an absolute slap in the face. 

My great Uncle was a messenger boy  in the Greek navy at the time. The family story is that he delivered a message to the captain and the captain began to cry. He told Panayioti (my uncle) that the Greek navy was ordered to leave and not protect the coast… my uncle ran home and told his mother they needed to flee immediately. She scooped up my great grandmother and the rest of her kids and they made it onto one of the boats. If my uncle hadn’t warned them in time, my family wouldn’t be here today. 

Many ships took as many refugees as they could, but as they left, many Greeks and Armenians died in the waters trying to escape the fires and the attackers. It was a horrible, violent event and it’s so hard to believe that people deny it to this day. Thank you so much for sharing this video.
